name: Netherlands
summary_text: Visa requirements for the Netherlands depend on nationality alone. Transgender and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications, and a passport carrying a gender marker other than the one assigned at birth, or an 'X' marker, is accepted for entry provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border.  Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited. Gender expression became an explicitly protected ground under the Equal Treatment Act in March 2019, following passage by the House of Representatives in 2018 (127 votes to 23) and the Senate on 12 March 2019 (64 to 11), after the Netherlands Institute for Human Rights had already treated transgender people as covered by the word 'gender' in earlier cases. Since February 2023, sexual orientation and disability are formally written into Article 1 of the Constitution.  Since 1 July 2025, a discriminatory motive is codified in Dutch law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, operating alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. Dutch legislation nonetheless contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime'; police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents through the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination (ECAD-P), which is the framework behind published hate-crime statistics.  Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.  During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.  Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.  Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.  Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.  Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

sources.detail: House passed Sept 2025 simple majority; Senate passed 16 June 2026; ratified 8 Sept 2026; prior TV expose Ewout & homogenezing RTL5 23 April 2019; Minister Hugo de Jonge letter May 2019; House motions 22 May 2019 to investigate and 29 May 2019 to legislate ban

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is rising. Police recorded 4,800 discrimination and violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year, up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022, with reports concerning transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399). The COC described the figures as extremely worrying and noted only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination in the same year. Official Dutch government figures state that over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, including 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people, and that incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism; in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation.  During WorldPride Amsterdam 2026, more than 70 people reported discrimination through the RITA platform in the opening period, mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants; RITA warned the reports are only a fraction of the total. Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride to cover the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. Mayor Femke Halsema told the council that Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride, with police, enforcer and organiser agreements to act fast; recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene.  Legal gender change in the Netherlands still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination. The 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking three to nine months, and the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025. Compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. Legal gender recognition has otherwise been administrative since a December 2013 law took effect in 2014, removing the earlier requirement of surgery and sterilisation imposed by the 1984-85 laws.  Transgender detainees occupy an unregulated space in Dutch law. No law, regulation or official policy governs their placement: the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees, and the Prison Service (DJI) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the municipal records (BRP) together with case-by-case factors such as gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, and physical or mental health. The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM) advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection, Robine van der Meer and later Minister Weerwind, in a letter of 21 February 2024 that this absence of rules is worrying and undesirable, noting international research documenting human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence against transgender detainees, the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees, and the relevance of CPT standards. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. Documented cases include a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing before transfer to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling of 21 March 2016 (15/4323/GB) concerning a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation; and rulings by the Limburg court (17 October 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624) and The Hague appeals court (29 June 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asked the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity; the DIZ said it was drafting guidelines, unpublished at the time.  Access to care: Dutch insurance fully covers PrPreP and related care for gay and bisexual men from 1 August 2019 at all Municipal Health Services (GGD) offices. Assisted insemination for infertility is covered by health insurance regardless of whether the patient is single, in an opposite-sex couple or a lesbian couple. The 2016 Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport guidelines, endorsed by eight medical organisations including the Dutch Psychiatry Association and Transvisie, recommend puberty blockers for transgender adolescents at Tanner Stage II with informed consent and endocrinologist approval, and top surgery is available to patients over 16. In July 2026 the Dutch Health Board reaffirmed gender-affirming care for trans youth, citing harms of delay, mental-health improvements and a low regret rate. Conversion therapy has been excluded from health insurance coverage since June 2012 and the practice was banned by a bill ratified on 8 September 2026.  Open military service has been permitted for gay people since homosexuality's declassification as a mental illness in 1973 and for transgender people as well. Equaldex records the Netherlands as recognising non-binary gender, protecting bathroom access, and prohibiting discrimination in employment and housing on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds, while noting that hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

name: Norway
summary_text: Norwegian law contains no offence targeting trans people. In November 2020 the Storting amended the Penal Code so that hate speech under Paragraph 135a covers bisexual and transgender people as well as sexual orientation; the amendment took effect in 2020 and Reuters reported it as an extension of criminal liability to anti-trans hate speech. The hate-crime framework recorded by OSCE/ODIHR defines hate crimes as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability, and any offence so motivated is recorded under that framework.  Legal gender recognition runs on self-declaration with no medical-intervention requirement. Under the Gender Recognition Act as set out on the official helsenorge.no health-rights page, the change of legal gender is decided at the tax office on the basis of the individual's own perception of their gender identity: from age 16 on the person's own application, between 6 and 16 with parental consent, and below 6 only for documented congenital differences of sex development. A 2017 regulation governs the document change for citizens resident abroad.  Gender-affirming healthcare does not follow the same self-declaration route. Access still requires a psychiatric diagnosis and referral to the National Treatment Centre for Gender Incongruence (NTCGI) at Oslo University Hospital, where only about a quarter of referred patients are admitted to treatment and those disqualified have no alternative options. A 2023 report found non-binary people still without treatment despite a 2020 guideline calling for equal access. For minors, 2020 guidelines recommend puberty blockers between Tanner stage 2 and age 16 following interdisciplinary assessment.  Reported hate crime is rising while clearance falls. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records an 18% increase in reported hate crimes in 2023, with the largest rises in offences motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, and antisemitism. NRK reported record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate dropped from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims told police they have little trust in the authorities, while a dedicated hate-crime group continues to encourage reporting. Official figures undercount by a wide margin: the HATECYCLE study at the University of Oslo surveyed more than 3,000 LGBTQI people and found that only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police, citing mistrust, procedural obstacles, fear of personal costs, and dismissive treatment by officers where reporting did occur.  Violence remains the principal offset to that legal position. A gunman killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022; the perpetrator, Zaniar Matapour, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years, the strictest penalty available. The same review period recorded a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime and online threats against a drag bingo event. The Police Security Service (PST) reported a significant decline in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, while warning that hate speech and intimidation risks persist, particularly during Pride, and that most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than to act.  Discrimination protection is long-standing and explicit as to gender identity. Norway was the first country to enact LGBT anti-discrimination law, amending Paragraph 349a of the Penal Code in 1981 to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation in goods and services and at public gatherings; employment discrimination on sexual grounds has been banned since 1998, and since 2013 Section 5 of the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination on the grounds of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression prohibits discrimination based on gender identity and expression. Norway is among the few countries explicitly protecting intersex people from discrimination. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 1 January 2009 with full rights including religious weddings, adoption and assisted reproduction, building on a registered partnership law from 1993 and recognition of unregistered same-sex cohabitation since 1991 for limited rights such as next-of-kin medical decisions; in 2024 Norway was ranked the best country in the world for same-sex couples to marry legally.
